The Banking Model

What teaching does to power

Education is never neutral: it either domesticates or liberates. Freire's claim, and the fight it started.

2 min read4 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected 2 timesUpdated 21 September 2026

In 1963, in the Brazilian town of Angicos, some three hundred farm workers learned to read in forty hours of lessons, given between January and April — starting from words they already carried: brick, work, land.

If you keep one line

Watch what a classroom trains people to do: receive deposits, or pose problems.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Paulo Freire's literacy method looked simple and wasn't. Instead of primers about Eva seeing the grape, his 'culture circles' began from generative words drawn from the workers' own lives — tijolo, brick, for construction labourers — broken into syllables and rebuilt into new words, while the circle discussed what bricks, work and land meant in their world. Reading arrived welded to the realisation that the world was made, and could be remade. The army noticed. After the 1964 coup Freire was jailed, then exiled for fifteen years.

'Pedagogy of the Oppressed', written in exile and published in English in 1970, names the enemy: banking education, in which the teacher deposits information into student-accounts who receive, file and store it. The alternative is problem-posing education — teacher and student investigating the world together — and the goal is conscientização: reading the word and the world at once. It became one of the most cited books in all of social science, and the founding text of critical pedagogy.

The critiques are serious, and not only hostile. The prose is dense with Hegel and hard to operationalise; the method travels badly without Freire-grade practitioners; the romance of 'the oppressed' can flatten the people it honours; and the strongest literacy evidence since points to structured, explicit instruction — deposits, as it were — for the mechanics of decoding. bell hooks, his most productive American inheritor, praised the liberation and named the blind spot: the sexism of the early text, which Freire later acknowledged.

And it became a culture-war object: assigned in thousands of education schools, banned from Tucson classrooms under Arizona's 2010 ethnic-studies law, waved as both bible and bogeyman by people who show no sign of having read it. Which is itself the cleanest demonstration of his thesis — nobody fights this hard over a neutral technology.

01By the numbers

40 hoursOf lessons at Angicos, January–April 1963, after which 300 of the 380 who began were certified literate: Instituto Paulo Freire, 'Angicos 50 Anos — Cronologia'
1970'Pedagogy of the Oppressed' appears in English, translated by Myra Bergman Ramos: Wikipedia, 'Pedagogy of the Oppressed'
15 yrsFreire's exile, from the 1964 coup to his first visit home in 1979 (counted to his 1980 return, sixteen): Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Paulo Freire'; Pedagogy and Theatre of the Oppressed, 'A Brief Biography of Paulo Freire'
3rdMost-cited book in the social sciences on Google Scholar, with 72,359 citations, behind Kuhn and Rogers: Elliott Green, 'What are the most-cited publications in the social sciences (according to Google Scholar)?', LSE Impact Blog, 2016

02How it happened

  1. 1963Angicos: some 300 workers reach basic literacy in forty hours of culture circles, January to April.
  2. 1964The military coup; Freire is jailed, then exiled — Bolivia, Chile, Geneva.
  3. 1968'Pedagogia do Oprimido' written in Chile; the English translation follows in 1970.
  4. 1980Freire returns to Brazil after amnesty.
  5. 1989Appointed secretary of education for São Paulo — theory meets a two-million-student system.
  6. 2010Arizona's HB 2281 leads to the book's removal from Tucson's dismantled ethnic-studies programme.

03Who did the work

Paulo FreireA lawyer turned literacy organiser who treated reading as a political act, and paid for it with exile.
Elza FreireTeacher and collaborator; the culture-circle method grew out of work they built together.
bell hooksCarried Freire into the American classroom, kept the liberation, and named the blind spots.

04Where it is contested

Almost everything: whether the method scales beyond charismatic practitioners, whether the empirical literacy evidence favours it (structured instruction has the stronger trial record for decoding), whether 'critical pedagogy' as practised keeps any of Freire's discipline, and — from his own allies — the early text's gender politics. The diagnosis wears better than the prescription.

05Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 8 · Sept 2026 · A source that did not exist.

The Banking Model of Education listed a Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Paulo Freire in its reading list. The Stanford Encyclopedia has no entry on Freire; he appears only inside other articles. The reading list now points to the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's entry, which does exist. The link had been dead since publication.

№ 10 · Sept 2026 · Angicos and the printing press.

The Banking Model of Education said Freire's workers at Angicos learned to read in forty-five days, and printed 45 days as a figure. The Paulo Freire Institute's own chronology has the lessons running from late January to early April 1963; the programme was named for its forty hours of instruction, after which 300 of the 380 who began were certified literate. The entry now says forty hours. Movable Type said Jeremiah Dittmar's estimate put the growth advantage of early-printing cities at 35 percentage points or more. The paper says over 30, and 35 appears nowhere in it. Both figures had been printed under the promise that they were sourced; neither line named where it came from, and both now do.

06What I changed my mind about

I came to Freire as an admirer and left as a friendly witness. 'Education is never neutral' survives every objection I have found; the specific method survives fewer. I now hold the two separately — which, since holding contradictions consciously is what he called critical consciousness, feels like the Freirean move.
